title: Two surfaces and the same water
stem: Constructed capillary-rise data were obtained in equal-bore tubes at the same temperature. Clean glass gave heights of 0, 18, 28 and 30 mm at 0, 10, 20 and 30 s. Wax-coated glass gave 0, 2, 3 and 3 mm. A separate photograph-free molecular schematic is not needed: distinguish the two intermolecular interactions in your explanation.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Calculate the mean rate of rise during the first 20 s in each tube and compare the rates.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain the contrast using both adhesion and cohesion.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Evaluate the claim that the results show water rises faster in every narrow biological pore.

steps.text: Divide each change in height by the same 20 s interval.
Clean glass: 28/20 = 1.4 mm s⁻¹; coated glass: 3/20 = 0.15 mm s⁻¹.
The clean-glass rate is about 9.3 times the coated-glass rate.
Adhesion is attraction between water and polar or charged sites on the glass; wax provides fewer favourable sites.
Cohesion is attraction between water molecules through hydrogen bonding.
Adhesion draws water along the surface while cohesion helps the neighbouring water column follow; adhesion and cohesion are different interactions.
The result is restricted to these surfaces and conditions; pore radius and surface chemistry in soil or cell walls can differ.
Test multiple biological materials at controlled bore size, temperature and water composition, with replicate tubes, before generalizing.

title: Cooling in two habitats
stem: In a constructed comparison, equal-temperature animal-shaped models initially at 35 °C are placed in air or water at 15 °C. Their surface materials and dimensions are identical. After 10 min, the air model is at 32 °C and the water model at 24 °C; after 20 min they are at 30 °C and 19 °C. Each model has heat capacity 500 J °C⁻¹, so energy lost = heat capacity × fall in temperature.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Calculate the mean rate of heat loss over the first 10 min for each model, in J min⁻¹.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain two challenges faced by a warm aquatic animal, using physical properties of water.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Explain why neither the graph nor the calculation directly measures the specific heat capacity of water.

steps.text: Use temperature falls of 3 °C in air and 11 °C in water with the stated heat capacity.
Water has higher thermal conductivity than air, so an uninsulated warm animal can lose heat more rapidly.
Insulation such as blubber reduces heat transfer and the energy needed to maintain body temperature.
Water is more viscous than air, creating greater resistance to movement; streamlining reduces drag.
The cooling objects are the models, whose heat capacity was supplied; the amount of surrounding water and its temperature change were not measured.
Convection, flow and the temperature difference also influence cooling, so conductivity alone is not isolated by these data.
Water’s high specific heat capacity means a given mass changes temperature relatively little for a given energy input, helping stabilize aquatic temperatures.

title: An air gap in a tensioned column
stem: Constructed data show water flow through matched leaf stalks under constant illumination. At 4 min an air bubble is introduced into one xylem vessel in the treatment stalk; a sham manipulation is made in the control. Flows at 0, 2, 4, 6, 8 min are respectively 12, 12, 12, 4, 5 μL min⁻¹ in the treatment and 12, 12, 12, 11, 12 μL min⁻¹ in the control. Each plotted value is a mean of five stalks; no uncertainty estimates are supplied.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Calculate the percentage decrease in treatment flow between 4 and 6 min and the difference from the control at 6 min.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain how molecular properties of water account for the treatment effect.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Evaluate the evidence that the bubble caused the decrease.

steps.text: Percentage decrease = (12 − 4)/12 × 100.
The decrease is 66.7%; treatment flow is 7 μL min⁻¹ lower than the control at 6 min.
Unequal electron sharing gives water partial charges, allowing intermolecular hydrogen bonds.
Cohesion allows a continuous column of water molecules to transmit tension along a vessel.
An air gap interrupts that continuous column, reducing transmission of tension and flow in the affected vessel.
The treatment changes after the manipulation while the sham control remains near its original flow, supporting an effect of the bubble.
Sham controls help separate the bubble from damage or disturbance during manipulation; identical leaf area and environmental conditions should also be controlled.
Means alone do not establish statistical significance; variability and replication must be assessed, and remaining flow could use other vessels.

title: Water delivery is not water retention
stem: A constructed planet comparison follows an equal mass of water delivered by asteroids. The graph gives the fraction still gravitationally retained after an early atmospheric-loss interval. Planet P has relative gravity 0.4, Q 1.0 and R 1.8. P and Q later cool to temperatures allowing water vapour to condense at their atmospheric pressures; R remains too hot for condensation. The displayed fractions are P 0.20, Q 0.75 and R 0.95. No independent evidence of organisms is supplied.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: If each received 8.0 × 10¹⁹ kg of water, calculate the retained masses for P and Q and their ratio.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain why R could retain the most water without having a liquid-water surface habitat.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Evaluate the claim that asteroid delivery alone explains a long-term environment suitable for life.

steps.text: Multiply the delivered mass by each retained fraction.
P retains 1.6 × 10¹⁹ kg; Q retains 6.0 × 10¹⁹ kg.
Q retains 3.75 times as much as P.
Greater gravity can help retain water or water vapour rather than allowing escape.
Retention alone does not imply liquid water; temperatures must permit condensation at the relevant pressure.
Under the supplied conditions, R’s retained water can remain vapour rather than forming liquid surface water.
Asteroids provide a plausible source of water, but delivery must be followed by retention and conditions allowing liquid water.
The comparison supports a role for gravity, but other properties could differ between planets; equal delivery is an explicit model assumption.
Liquid water is relevant as a solvent and reaction medium, but its presence would not demonstrate that life had originated.

steps.text: The overlap is from the larger inner boundary, 1.10 AU, to the smaller outer boundary, 1.40 AU.
The 1.25 AU planet lies inside both zones; overlap width =1.40 −1.10 =0.30 AU.
Liquid water dissolves many biologically relevant substances and provides a medium for reactions.
At distances that are too hot or too cold under the model conditions, stable liquid surface water is less likely.

A planet must first obtain water, for example by asteroid delivery; the zone does not establish its water inventory.
Gravity must be sufficient to limit water loss, and the actual atmosphere and temperature must permit condensation.

title: A composition claim for a DNA fragment
stem: A constructed double-stranded DNA fragment contains 120 base pairs and 48 adenine nucleotides in total. The diagram shows only a short representative section, not the entire fragment. A student claims that the fragment must contain equal quantities of all four bases.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Deduce the number of thymine, guanine and cytosine nucleotides in the whole fragment.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain why the student’s conclusion does not follow from complementary base pairing.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Compare the fragment with an RNA polymer containing 120 nucleotides, and explain why its base totals need not obey the same equalities.

steps.text: There are 240 nucleotides in 120 base pairs; total A equals total T and total G equals total C.
T =48; the remaining 144 nucleotides are G and C, so G =72 and C =72.
A pairs with T and G pairs with C, so complementarity constrains paired totals rather than requiring all four totals to match.
The order and relative frequencies of A–T and G–C pairs can vary along a DNA molecule.
Different sequences permit genetic information to vary even when two molecules have the same overall base composition.
RNA contains ribose and uracil rather than deoxyribose and thymine.
A single RNA strand is not constrained by a complete complementary strand, so A need not equal U and G need not equal C.
Both polymers have a covalently linked sugar–phosphate backbone; hydrogen bonding links complementary bases rather than making that backbone.

title: Assembling an RNA chain
stem: The schematic represents five free RNA nucleotides before formation of one unbranched chain. Each is labelled P for phosphate, S for pentose sugar and with its base. Assume each linkage forms by condensation, releasing one water molecule, and no circular chain is formed.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Calculate the number of condensation linkages and water molecules released, and explain why these differ from the number of nucleotides.

parts.label: b

parts.label: c

steps.text: Joining n separate units into one linear chain requires n −1 joins.
Five nucleotides require four linkages and release four water molecules.
Phosphate and ribose units alternate in the covalent backbone.
Each nitrogenous base remains attached to its own sugar and is not placed within the backbone.
The base order A, U, G, C, A is preserved, with one unbranched strand and terminal groups remaining at its ends.
The sequences differ, so the same base totals do not establish the same information.
RNA uses ribose and uracil; DNA uses deoxyribose and thymine.
DNA is normally double-stranded whereas the represented RNA chain is single-stranded; do not claim that RNA can never contain paired regions.

title: A shared code is evidence, not identity
stem: In a constructed comparison, the same four RNA triplets are tested in a plant, a fungus and a bacterium. The figure represents supplied results: UUU specifies phenylalanine, GGU glycine, UAC tyrosine and CAA glutamine in all three. The organisms nevertheless make different proteins from many of their own genes. Detailed translation mechanisms are not required.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Explain how the results support common ancestry without showing that the three genomes are identical.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: A student says that identical code use means identical proteins. Use the supplied code to refute this claim with two different three-triplet sequences.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Evaluate the extent to which the four triplets establish universality of the genetic code.

steps.text: The same triplets specifying the same amino acids in different groups is consistent with inheritance of a shared genetic code.
Common ancestry can account for that conserved coding relationship.
The code describes the meaning of triplets, whereas genomes can differ in triplet sequence, gene content and regulation.
Construct two valid sequences from the supplied triplets that differ in their order or composition.
For example UUU–GGU–CAA gives phenylalanine–glycine–glutamine, whereas CAA–GGU–UUU gives glutamine–glycine–phenylalanine; another correct pair is acceptable.
Only four triplets and three organisms were tested, so the sample does not establish all coding assignments in all life.
Broader sampling of organisms and triplets would strengthen the inference; the code is near-universal rather than necessarily identical in every context.
Independent sequence or cellular evidence should be combined with code conservation; these results alone do not prove a detailed evolutionary relationship.

title: Which direction does the message run?
stem: The schematic gives a DNA segment. Its lower strand is the template read during transcription from left to right. Supplied RNA assignments are AUG=methionine, GCU=alanine, UAC=tyrosine and UAA=stop. Assume transcription begins at the leftmost displayed template base and the reading frame begins at the first RNA base.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Write the RNA sequence with both end labels, then give the amino acid sequence before termination.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain why writing the same RNA bases in reverse order without changing the end labels is incorrect.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Describe the backbone linkage and explain why complementary base pairing does not itself hold each single strand together.

steps.text: Read template 3′–TACCGAATGATT–5′ continuously as TAC–CGA–ATG–ATT and apply complementary RNA pairing.
The RNA is 5′–AUG–GCU–UAC–UAA–3′.
The peptide sequence is methionine–alanine–tyrosine; UAA is a stop signal, not an amino acid.
The two DNA strands are antiparallel and RNA is synthesized in the 5′ to 3′ direction while the template is read 3′ to 5′.
Reversal with fixed end labels changes the oriented sequence and therefore the grouping or identity of codons.
Successive nucleotides are joined by covalent sugar–phosphate linkages involving the 3′ position of one sugar and 5′ position of the next nucleotide.
Hydrogen bonds occur between complementary bases on paired strands, rather than replacing covalent backbone bonds.
Different base sequences retain the same directional backbone organization, allowing information to vary without changing its basic chemical framework.

title: Keeping the width of a DNA helix
stem: In a simplified constructed geometry model, purine bases A and G each contribute 0.60 nm to a pair width and pyrimidines C and T each contribute 0.40 nm. These are model dimensions, not measured atomic dimensions. The diagram compares A–T, G–C, A–G and C–T pairings. Only the usual complementary pairs are assumed to form normal DNA base pairs.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Calculate the model width of each pairing and identify which alternatives make the helix wider or narrower.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain how purine–pyrimidine pairing permits sequence diversity with a relatively uniform helix width.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Evaluate the inference that any pair with width 1.00 nm must be a stable complementary pair.

steps.text: Add the contributions of the two bases in each pair.
A–T and G–C are each 1.00 nm; A–G is 1.20 nm and C–T is 0.80 nm.
A and G are purines whereas C and T are pyrimidines.
Each usual complementary pair combines one purine with one pyrimidine, giving equal overall width.
The relative order of A–T and G–C pairs can therefore vary while the helix retains a consistent overall geometry.
Width alone is insufficient; the arrangement of hydrogen-bond donors and acceptors must also allow appropriate interactions.
The model uses only approximate base size and omits detailed three-dimensional chemistry.
Normal complementarity is A–T and G–C; no claim that arbitrary equal-width pairs behave identically follows from the model.

title: A repeat unit of chromatin
stem: The constructed chromatin schematic shows three complete repeat units. In the supplied model, each repeat contains 146 base pairs wrapped around an eight-histone core and 54 base pairs of linker DNA, with one linker histone associated with each repeat. Ignore end effects and assume all repeat units are complete.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Calculate the number of core histone proteins, linker histones and DNA base pairs in 25 repeats.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Describe the organization that distinguishes a nucleosome from free histones mixed with DNA.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Explain why the number of nucleosomes alone cannot determine the genetic information in the DNA.

steps.text: Scale each repeat component by 25; 146 +54 =200 base pairs per repeat.
There are 200 core histone proteins and 25 linker histones.
The DNA contains 5000 base pairs in total.
DNA is wrapped around a core containing eight histone proteins, not enclosed inside a histone membrane.
Linker DNA connects neighbouring core-associated DNA segments.
A further linker histone is associated with the linker/core arrangement; the core itself is still an octamer.
The number specifies packaging units or an approximate DNA length under this model, not base order.
Different base sequences can have the same length and number of nucleosome repeats.

title: Tracer recovery and an alternative explanation
stem: A constructed repeat of a phage-label experiment uses phosphorus-labelled DNA or sulfur-labelled protein in separate batches. After infection, blending and centrifugation, the figure shows recovered tracer in the bacterial pellet and supernatant. DNA-labelled batch: pellet 72%, supernatant 24%; protein-labelled batch: pellet 8%, supernatant 88%; the remainder was not recovered. A non-infected labelled-phage control has 5% of supplied tracer in the pellet.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Calculate the unrecovered fraction and the pellet fraction of recovered tracer for each infected batch.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain how the contrast supports DNA rather than protein as the inherited phage material.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Evaluate a claim that every pellet-associated label atom must have entered a cell.

steps.text: Unrecovered tracer is 100 − (pellet + supernatant); normalize pellet to total recovered.
Both batches lose 4%; DNA pellet fraction =72/96 =75.0% and protein pellet fraction =8/96 =8.33%.
Phosphorus labels the DNA and sulfur labels sulfur-containing protein, allowing the components to be followed separately.
Most recovered DNA label is associated with bacterial cells while most protein label is outside them after blending.
This is consistent with DNA entering cells and carrying information for production of progeny phages; entry alone is supportive evidence, not the complete inheritance mechanism.
The 5% pellet signal without infection shows some label can pellet without intracellular entry, for example by external association.
The 8% protein pellet signal could include residual external phage material; blending may be incomplete.

Controls for free label, cell integrity and phage attachment, and tracing label into progeny, would strengthen interpretation; do not subtract the control as a proven exact correction for every batch.

title: What did the discharge chamber establish?
stem: A constructed closed-chamber experiment supplies the same inorganic carbon input to each treatment. After 48 h, organic-product carbon is measured. Reducing gas mixture with electrical discharge: 18 mg; the same mixture without discharge: 2 mg; a second plausible atmosphere with discharge: 6 mg; reagent blank: 1 mg. All apparatus was sterilized and three independent runs gave the stated means; no living cells were detected.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Calculate net organic-product carbon above the blank in the first and third treatments and their ratio.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain what the discharge and atmosphere comparisons contribute to the hypothesis of abiotic organic synthesis.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Evaluate the claim that the experiment created life and reconstructed the exact origin of cells.

steps.text: Subtract 1 mg from both relevant measured values.
The net products are 17 mg and 5 mg; the first is 3.4 times the third.
Organic carbon above the blank in a sterile system is consistent with formation from non-living inputs.
The same-mixture comparison supports a role for energy supplied by the discharge.
Different yields in the two atmospheres show that conclusions depend on the assumed early-Earth gas composition.
Organic molecules are not self-sustaining cells; catalysis, replication, self-assembly and compartmentalization must also be explained.
Early-Earth conditions cannot be reconstructed exactly, so these are model tests of plausibility rather than direct historical observation.
Sterilization and blanks reduce contamination concerns but further chemical identification and independent replication are needed; no cells were observed.

title: A compartment can retain a catalyst
stem: Constructed fatty-acid vesicles initially contain 100 arbitrary units of RNA catalyst. After free external RNA is removed, vesicle-associated RNA is 100, 72 and 54 units at 0, 30 and 60 min. With a membrane-disrupting treatment it is 100, 12 and 2 units. An external large dye that cannot cross intact bilayers becomes associated with disrupted but not intact vesicles. No RNA copying was measured.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Calculate the percentage retained at 60 min in each treatment and the fold difference.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain how fatty-acid self-assembly could help the origin of cellular life.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Evaluate whether retention demonstrates a living protocell.

steps.text: Use the common initial quantity 100 as denominator.
Intact vesicles retain 54%; disrupted vesicles retain 2%; the ratio is 27.
Fatty acids can self-assemble into bilayer-bounded vesicles in suitable conditions.
A boundary creates a compartment whose chemical composition can differ from the surroundings.
Retention can concentrate interacting molecules or catalysts, allowing internal reactions rather than immediate dispersal.
Retention and the dye result support a functional barrier, but the vesicles still leak RNA over time.
There is no evidence here of self-replication, heritable change or self-sustaining metabolism.
Measure repeated RNA copying and compartment growth/division with appropriate no-catalyst controls before inferring more of the prerequisites for life.

title: A molecule that copies and catalyses
stem: In a constructed cell-free system, an RNA molecule catalyses formation of a short product. Active RNA gives 0, 12, 24 and 36 nmol at 0, 10, 20 and 30 min; an equal amount of sequence-scrambled RNA gives 0, 1, 2 and 3 nmol. In a separate supplied assay, an RNA template can be copied using added activated nucleotides and a laboratory catalyst. Neither assay is inside a growing compartment.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Calculate the mean product-formation rate in each assay and the ratio of rates.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain why RNA is a plausible candidate for an early genetic material, using both assays.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: State three limitations of the inference that RNA alone has been shown to generate living cells.

steps.text: Divide the 30-min change in product by 30 min.
Active RNA gives 1.2 nmol min⁻¹ and scrambled RNA 0.10 nmol min⁻¹, a 12-fold difference.
RNA base sequence can store information and complementary pairing can support copying.
The product assay supports catalytic activity that depends on RNA sequence.
An RNA-based system could therefore combine information storage and some catalysis without initially requiring a separate protein catalyst for every function.
The copying assay uses a supplied laboratory catalyst and activated inputs; autonomous self-copying has not been demonstrated.
The separate assays do not show that the same RNA copies itself while retaining catalytic function.
Compartmentalization, sustained energy/input supply and repeated reproduction with heritable variation are not established.

title: Fossils constrain a minimum, not an exact origin
stem: A constructed timeline uses ages before the present. Earth forms at 4.54 billion years ago (Ga). A rock contains structures independently assessed as biological and dated 3.48 ±0.04 Ga; uncertainty bounds are supplied as possible ages, not confidence intervals. A genomic model estimates LUCA at 3.80–4.10 Ga. Geological dating and the genomic model are independent lines of evidence.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Calculate the interval between Earth’s formation and the central rock age, and the youngest age permitted by the rock bounds.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain what the fossil evidence can establish about the date of the first cells.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Distinguish LUCA from the first life and evaluate whether the two estimates conflict.

steps.text: Subtract the rock age from 4.54 Ga and subtract 0.04 Ga from 3.48 Ga.
The interval is 1.06 billion years; the youngest permitted rock age is 3.44 Ga.
If the structures are biological and contemporaneous with the rock, life existed by the rock’s age.
The earliest preserved evidence need not be the earliest life because preservation and discovery are incomplete.
Thus the fossil gives a minimum age for life, conservatively at least 3.44 Ga under these supplied bounds, rather than its exact origin date.
LUCA is the last common ancestor of all currently surviving cellular lineages, not necessarily the first organism.
Earlier lineages could have existed and become extinct, and descendants of LUCA could produce younger fossils.
A LUCA estimate older than this fossil is therefore compatible with it; model assumptions and fossil interpretation still require evaluation.

title: Two lines of evidence near hydrothermal vents
stem: Constructed evidence consists of ancient filament-like structures in seafloor vent precipitates and reconstructed ancestral enzyme activity. The graph shows activity at 40, 60, 80 and 100 °C: 20, 65, 100 and 35 units. Shared gene sequences across widely separated cellular groups were used to infer the ancestral sequence. Some non-biological minerals can also form filaments.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Describe the temperature response and calculate activity at 100 °C as a percentage of the maximum observed activity.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain how the geological and genomic observations could jointly support a vent-associated LUCA.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Evaluate two alternative explanations or limitations.

steps.text: Identify the maximum observed value 100 units at 80 °C.
Activity increases from 40 to 80 °C, then falls; at 100 °C it is 35% of the observed maximum.
Ancient vent deposits could preserve evidence that early life occupied vent environments, if the structures are genuinely biological.
Conserved sequences allow a model of ancestral proteins, and high activity at elevated temperatures is compatible with a warm ancestral environment.
Independent geological and molecular evidence can strengthen a common interpretation, while neither alone locates LUCA with certainty.
Mineral filaments could imitate biological structures, so chemical, structural and contextual tests are needed to assess origin.
Ancestral sequence reconstruction and temperature preference depend on the sampled sequences and model; present-day descendants are not LUCA itself.
The observed optimum is among four tested temperatures, not an exact optimum, and heat tolerance alone does not uniquely identify hydrothermal vents.

title: Calibrating before measuring
stem: At a fixed microscope objective, 30 eyepiece divisions coincide with 12 stage-micrometer intervals. Each stage interval represents 10 μm. A cell spans 18 eyepiece divisions. At a second objective the same 120 μm length spans 60 eyepiece divisions. The calibration diagram is schematic, with corresponding end points aligned.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Calculate the calibration at the second objective and predict the divisions occupied by the same cell.

parts.label: c

steps.text: The known stage length is 12 ×10 =120 μm, so divide 120 by 30.
One eyepiece division is 4.0 μm; the cell length is 18 ×4.0 =72 μm.
The new calibration is 120/60 =2.0 μm per division.
The 72 μm cell would span 36 eyepiece divisions, provided it has the same orientation and boundaries.
Changing the objective changes the eyepiece calibration, so a larger image does not establish biological growth.
Using 4 μm per division at the second objective would give 144 μm, twice the actual length.
Calibrate each objective and retain magnification-independent scale bars or actual dimensions when comparing images.
Identify consistent cell boundaries and repeat measurements across cells; orientation and preparation can also affect apparent length.

title: Resolving two neighbouring structures
stem: The constructed diagram places two fluorescent targets 150 nm apart. Instrument L has a stated resolution limit 200 nm and instrument E 2 nm; assume features closer than the limit cannot be resolved separately. Enlarging an L image changes its printed width from 40 to 160 mm but does not add information. Instrument E requires fixed non-living material, while L can track a suitable fluorescent marker in living cells.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Determine which instrument can resolve the targets and calculate the enlargement factor of the printed L image.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain why the enlarged L image still cannot establish that there are two separate targets.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Design a complementary use of the instruments to investigate location and movement, identifying two limitations.

steps.text: L cannot distinguish targets 150 nm apart under the stated 200 nm criterion; E can under its 2 nm criterion.
The printed enlargement factor is 160/40 =4.0.
Resolution is the ability to distinguish close objects, whereas magnification makes an existing image larger.
Enlargement expands the unresolved combined signal and cannot recover spatial information not recorded by the instrument.
Use L with a specific fluorescent marker to follow changes in position in living cells over time.
Use E to examine fine structural separation in fixed samples, with scale bars and appropriately comparable regions.
The fixed E samples do not show movement directly, and preparation may alter structure.
A fluorescent signal identifies a labelled target only if marker specificity and controls are validated; fluorescence alone is not a full organelle structure image.

title: Two cells, one set of universal functions
stem: The schematic represents a Gram-positive bacterium P and a typical animal cell Q. In P, X is a loop of DNA free in the cytoplasm and Y represents small ribosomes. In Q, N encloses DNA behind a double membrane and Z is a membrane-bound compartment. The drawing is not to the same scale for the two cells.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Identify two structural contrasts and explain why they do not imply that P lacks genetic control or protein synthesis.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: State the ribosome type expected in the cytoplasm of each, and identify two other common cellular components.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Explain why this diagram cannot support a claim that all living cells contain a nucleus or have the same dimensions.

steps.text: P has no membrane-bounded nucleus, whereas Q contains a nucleus.
P lacks the represented membrane-bound cytoplasmic organelles; Q is compartmentalized.
P still has DNA carrying genetic information and ribosomes that synthesize proteins; absence of a nucleus does not mean absence of DNA.
P has 70S ribosomes and Q has 80S cytoplasmic ribosomes.
Both have a plasma membrane and an aqueous cytoplasm.
P provides a cellular example without a nucleus, so a nucleus is not universal.
The drawing explicitly uses different schematic scales, so drawn sizes cannot establish actual size equality.
Both organisms can carry out life processes as cells; the shared cellular organization, rather than a nucleus, underlies cell theory.

title: Counting nuclei does not count cells
stem: The constructed schematic shows a continuous skeletal muscle fibre with eight nuclei, an aseptate fungal hypha segment with six nuclei, a mature mammalian erythrocyte without a nucleus and a mature sieve-tube element without a nucleus. Membrane or wall boundaries, where present, are drawn; these structures are not all shown at the same scale.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Explain why dividing the total number of nuclei by one would not give a valid cell count in this sample.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain why the two anucleate examples do not refute the statement that cells arise from pre-existing cells.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Evaluate the rule that a single visible boundary and nucleus are always sufficient to identify a complete cell in a thin section.

steps.text: A muscle fibre can contain several nuclei within one continuous cell.
An aseptate hypha has many nuclei in continuous cytoplasm without cross walls dividing each nucleus into a separate cell.
A mature erythrocyte or sieve-tube element can be a specialized living cell even though it has no nucleus.
They develop from precursor cells that contained nuclei, so nuclear loss occurs during specialization.
Their origin remains cellular division and differentiation rather than spontaneous assembly from non-living matter.
A section can miss the nucleus or cut through only part of a cell, so absence in that section is not proof of nuclear absence.
Membrane continuity and adjacent sections or three-dimensional imaging can distinguish one extended cell from several neighbouring cells.
The atypical examples show that nuclear number is useful evidence but not a universal one-nucleus-per-cell definition.

title: Testing an endosymbiotic interpretation
stem: The constructed cell diagram contains mitochondria and chloroplasts. Supplied observations show circular DNA, 70S ribosomes and division of each organelle independently of nuclear division. A treatment that selectively inhibits 70S ribosomes reduces newly synthesized organelle-encoded proteins to 25% of control; newly synthesized cytoplasmic proteins remain 95% of control. Assume the treatment has the stated specificity.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Calculate the percentage reduction in each protein measurement and compare the reductions.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain how three observations support an endosymbiotic origin.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Evaluate whether the observations prove that modern free-living bacteria were the direct ancestors of these organelles.

steps.text: Subtract each treated percentage from 100%.
Organelle-encoded protein synthesis falls 75%; cytoplasmic synthesis falls 5%, a 70-percentage-point difference.
Circular organelle DNA resembles the circular DNA of bacterial cells and provides a partly independent genome.
70S ribosomes and the selective inhibition pattern are consistent with a bacterial-like protein-synthesis system.
Replication of organelles from pre-existing organelles is consistent with descent from incorporated cells rather than repeated de novo manufacture.
They support descent from ancestral bacteria, not identity with any present-day bacterial species.
Multiple independent features give stronger support than a single resemblance, but historical ancestry remains an inference.
Compare organelle and bacterial gene sequences to test relatedness; the drug response alone cannot identify the ancestral lineage.

title: Same genome, different cell roles
stem: Constructed expression measurements compare three cell types from one cloned plant. All three retain the same assayed DNA sequences. Relative RNA abundances for a photosynthesis gene P, transport gene T and housekeeping gene H are: leaf cells 90, 10, 50; transport cells 5, 85, 50; unspecialized cells 10, 10, 50. After a supplied developmental signal, descendants of the unspecialized cells show P 80, T 8, H 50. Values are relative units, not direct protein measurements.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Calculate the fold change in P expression after the signal and identify the most stable assayed gene.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain how the evidence supports differentiation through altered gene expression rather than loss of unwanted genes.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Evaluate the claim that the signal alone has been shown to cause complete leaf-cell differentiation.

title: Division of labour in a model colony
stem: A constructed colony contains motile outer cells and reproductive inner cells. After equal-time culture, intact colonies produce 80 viable daughter colonies per 100 starting colonies; removal of outer cells gives 20 and removal of inner cells gives 2. Sham-treated colonies give 76. Separate comparative evidence places multicellular animals, fungi and several algae in distinct lineages with unicellular relatives. No common multicellular ancestor is assumed by the data.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Calculate daughter-colony production relative to intact colonies for both removal treatments.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain how the results are consistent with an advantage of multicellularity.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Evaluate the evidence for repeated origins of multicellularity and the experimental interpretation.

steps.text: Divide each treatment output by 80 and multiply by 100.
Outer-cell removal gives 25% of intact production; inner-cell removal gives 2.5%.
Different cells can specialize in functions such as movement and reproduction within a larger unit.
Reduced output after outer-cell removal is compatible with motile cells helping the colony obtain favourable conditions or resources for reproduction.
The much lower output without inner cells is consistent with their reproductive role, allowing division of labour rather than every cell performing every function equally.
Multicellular groups separated by unicellular lineages are consistent with multiple origins; the experimental output itself does not reconstruct that history.
Removal could damage remaining cells or reduce colony size, so sham operations and equal-size controls are necessary.
The sham output 76 is near 80, but uncertainty and replicate cultures are needed before claiming statistical equivalence or significance.

title: A one-step phage growth curve
stem: In a constructed synchronized lytic infection, 1000 bacterial cells are infected by lambda phage and unadsorbed phages are removed. Extracellular infectious phages remain near zero through 20 min, rise to 40000 at 30 min and reach 60000 at 40 min, remaining there at 50 min. Assume all 1000 infected cells lyse once, no secondary infections occur and infectious phages are counted without loss.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Estimate the time interval containing the start of phage release and calculate the mean burst size.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain why extracellular phage counts can remain low while infection is progressing.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Evaluate two assumptions needed to infer the burst size from the plateau.

steps.text: Release begins after 20 min and by 30 min; the sampling does not locate an exact release time.
Divide the plateau 60000 phages by 1000 lysed cells.
The mean burst size is 60 infectious phages per infected cell.
The phage genome enters the host and directs production of viral components using host resources.
Replication and assembly occur inside the cell before lysis releases infectious particles.
The extracellular count therefore does not measure all intracellular viral genomes or incomplete particles.
Secondary infections must be prevented; otherwise later release could be counted as output from the first infected cells.
The number of cells actually infected and lysed must be known, and phage decay or incomplete detection would lower the apparent burst size.

title: A prophage can persist without immediate lysis
stem: The schematic contrasts two fates of a lambda genome. In a constructed culture initially containing 2000 lysogenic bacterial cells, the prophage is copied with the bacterial chromosome. Following a DNA-damaging stimulus, 30% of cells enter a lytic cycle; assume the other cells survive. Each induced cell releases 50 infectious phages. No cell division or secondary infection occurs during the counting interval.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Calculate the number of induced cells, surviving lysogenic cells and released phages.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain how a viral genome can be inherited through bacterial divisions without release of infectious particles at every division.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Evaluate the assertion that a low free-phage count proves that a bacterial population is free of phage genomes.

steps.text: Induced cells =0.30 ×2000 =600; surviving lysogens =2000 −600.
There are 1400 surviving lysogens and 600 ×50 =30000 released phages.
During lysogeny, the phage DNA is integrated into the host chromosome as a prophage.
Replication of the bacterial chromosome also copies the prophage and passes it to daughter cells.
Lysis and particle release occur after induction into the lytic pathway rather than necessarily during each normal bacterial division.
Lysogens can carry integrated genomes while producing few or no extracellular infectious particles.
A genome-specific test or a controlled induction assay could reveal prophage carriage.
Failure of induction would not alone exclude a prophage if the stimulus or assay was ineffective; positive and negative controls are needed.

title: Different viral coverings
stem: Constructed schematics compare particle V, with RNA inside a protein capsid and an outer lipid envelope, with particle W, containing DNA in a protein capsid without an envelope. Both lack ribosomes. In a supplied selective assay, a lipid-disrupting agent leaves V at 5% infectivity and W at 92% of untreated controls. The agent does not damage the host cells in this model.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Calculate the percentage reduction in infectivity for each particle and compare the reductions.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain how the structural evidence could account for the treatment effect, without claiming all viruses have the same structure.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Explain why both particles depend on host cells despite containing genetic information.

steps.text: Reduction =100 minus infectivity remaining.
V falls 95% and W 8%; the reduction for V is 87 percentage points greater.
V’s lipid envelope can be disrupted, preventing an envelope-dependent interaction needed for infection.
W lacks a lipid envelope, so the selective agent has much less direct effect under the supplied conditions.
Viruses vary in DNA/RNA genomes and envelope presence; neither all-enveloped nor all-DNA is a valid universal description.
Neither has ribosomes for independent protein synthesis.
Replication and assembly depend on host cellular resources, so a genome and capsid alone do not constitute self-sustaining cellular life.
Residual infectivity or its loss should be measured with matched untreated and host-toxicity controls; structure alone does not quantify infectivity.

title: Selection among influenza variants
stem: In constructed influenza populations, a pre-existing variant begins at 2% frequency. With an antiviral treatment its frequency after passages 0, 1, 2, 3 is 2%, 10%, 35%, 70%; in a matched untreated population it is 2%, 2%, 3%, 3%. At the start, treated and untreated populations have equal variant frequencies. The variant has reduced drug sensitivity in a separate supplied assay. Population sizes are large, but replicate trajectories are not shown.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Calculate the fold increase in variant frequency under treatment and the final frequency difference between conditions.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain how selection can produce this pattern without the treatment directing an adaptive mutation.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Evaluate the claim that the data determine the mutation rate or prove that every influenza lineage will follow this trajectory.

steps.text: Compare 70% with 2%, and subtract 3% from 70%.
The frequency rises 35-fold; the final difference is 67 percentage points.
The variant was already present before treatment, so the drug need not create the useful variant.
Reduced sensitivity can allow the variant to leave more successful descendants than competing variants during treatment.
Repeated reproduction changes the population’s heritable composition, increasing variant frequency.
Frequency change combines reproduction, survival and potentially mutation; the mutation rate was not measured directly.
One trajectory does not establish repeatability; starting composition, host conditions and chance may affect outcomes.
Replicate populations with matched conditions and sequence tracking would strengthen the inference, while the untreated comparison supports a treatment-associated advantage.

title: Why one viral origin is not established
stem: The constructed gene trees show relationships for two viral genes and three cellular lineages. For gene X, viral sequence V is closest to cellular lineage A; for gene Y, viral sequence W is closest to cellular lineage C. Assume the trees are well supported for these genes. V and W are different virus groups; no universal viral gene shared by all viruses has been identified in this exercise.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Describe the two gene relationships and explain why they do not by themselves define one tree for all viruses.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Discuss how the evidence could be consistent with multiple origins of viruses or convergence on parasitism.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Give two further tests and explain the appropriate certainty of the conclusion.

steps.text: X places V with A, whereas Y places W with C.
The trees concern different genes and virus groups, so their roots and branching patterns cannot simply be merged into a universal virus ancestry.
Gene transfer or independent gene recruitment can make a gene history differ from a complete lineage history.
Different viral groups may have acquired genetic material from different cellular sources.
Host-dependent replication and protective capsids could arise in separate lineages under similar selective pressures.
Shared parasitic features alone therefore need not imply a single cellular-like common ancestor for all viruses.
Compare many independent viral and host genes, genome organization and structural proteins to assess whether the same relationships recur.
Evaluate transfer, loss and alternative tree reconstructions; the supplied observations support hypotheses rather than proving a unique historical origin.

title: Testing a chromosome-fusion hypothesis
stem: The constructed chromosome schematic aligns human chromosome 2 with two chromosomes from a chimpanzee-like comparison. Corresponding band blocks are labelled a, b, c, d. The human chromosome has the blocks in the same order plus an internal telomere-like sequence and a remnant second centromere. Humans have 46 chromosomes and chimpanzees 48. Detailed band patterns are supplied, not required recall.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Explain how a fusion in one ancestral chromosome set could account for the diploid-count difference.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain how three independent structural observations strengthen the fusion hypothesis.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Evaluate whether the comparison proves that modern chimpanzees were human ancestors.

steps.text: Joining two chromosomes into one reduces the chromosome number by one per haploid set.
When both homologous sets contain the fusion, the diploid number is reduced by two, consistent with 48 to 46.
Matching band blocks in the same order support correspondence between the single chromosome and the two ancestral components.
An internal telomere-like sequence is consistent with a former chromosome-end junction.
A remnant second centromere is consistent with a chromosome formed from two centromere-bearing ancestors.
The evidence is consistent with descent from a shared primate ancestor, not descent from the modern chimpanzee population.
Sequence mapping and comparisons with additional primates can test the proposed junction and ancestral arrangement.
Similar appearance alone would be weaker evidence; a testable fusion hypothesis predicts multiple corresponding features.

title: Genome size is not a ladder of complexity
stem: A constructed dataset gives haploid genome sizes: unicellular species U 0.020 Gb, insect I 0.18 Gb, mammal M 3.2 Gb and flowering plant F 24 Gb. These values describe invented organisms and are not estimates for named species. A genome includes coding and non-coding DNA; no proportions are supplied.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Calculate the ratio of F to M genome size and convert U’s genome size to megabases, using 1 Gb =1000 Mb.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain why the values cannot rank the organisms reliably by structural or functional complexity.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Evaluate whether equal genome sizes would establish species identity.

steps.text: Divide 24 by 3.2 and multiply 0.020 by 1000.
F has 7.5 times M’s DNA amount per haploid genome; U has 20 Mb.
Genome size is total DNA amount rather than the number of cell types, organs or behaviours.
Non-coding and repeated DNA can contribute substantially to genome size.
Gene content, sequence and expression patterns can differ without a proportional change in total DNA amount.
Different sequences can contain the same number of bases, so size alone does not identify a genome.
Within-species genomes share most information but can have sequence variation; between-species comparisons need more than length.
Sequence comparisons and other biological evidence are needed, with methods and sampling stated rather than assuming a universal size threshold.

title: A boundary between diverging populations
stem: Two constructed beetle populations P and Q differ slightly in body markings. In controlled crosses, viable adult offspring per 100 eggs are P×P 88, Q×Q 86 and P×Q 80. Of those surviving adults, the percentages producing fertile offspring when given suitable mates are 95%, 94% and 60%, respectively. No field mating frequencies are known. The figure plots adult survival and fertility separately, so fertility is not a percentage of eggs.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Estimate the number of fertile hybrid adults expected per 100 hybrid-cross eggs, assuming the supplied proportions apply.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Discuss whether the laboratory results establish that P and Q are separate biological species.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Explain why a morphological species decision might differ and suggest further evidence.

steps.text: First obtain 80 viable adults, then apply 60% fertility to those adults.
The expected number is 80 ×0.60 =48 fertile hybrid adults per 100 eggs.
Production of some fertile hybrids indicates that complete reproductive isolation has not been shown under laboratory conditions.
Reduced hybrid fertility compared with within-population crosses indicates partial divergence or a reproductive barrier.
Laboratory opportunities need not match natural mate choice or contact, so field gene exchange remains uncertain.
Morphological classification emphasizes shared or distinct traits, which may not coincide exactly with reproductive compatibility.
Speciation is often gradual, making the boundary between populations and species difficult to place.

title: A key that still works without colour
stem: Four invented leaf-bearing plants are represented by the schematic. P has opposite simple leaves, Q alternate simple leaves, R opposite compound leaves and S alternate compound leaves. Green colour varies with age and is not diagnostic. Assume the four supplied structural states are stable and that every specimen belongs to exactly one of these taxa.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Construct a dichotomous key that identifies all four taxa using only the supplied stable traits.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain why a key beginning “green leaves” versus “large leaves” is invalid.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: A damaged specimen retains only one compound leaf and no visible leaf attachment pattern. State the defensible identification and explain a way to improve it.

steps.text: Start with one paired contrast, for example simple leaves versus compound leaves.
For simple leaves, opposite gives P and alternate gives Q.
For compound leaves, opposite gives R and alternate gives S; a valid arrangement using leaf position first is equally acceptable.
The alternatives are not mutually exclusive opposites: a leaf can be both green and large.
Colour is stated to vary with age, and no size criterion is supplied, so these features do not reliably separate the taxa.
The specimen can be narrowed to R or S but cannot be uniquely identified from the retained evidence.
Observe intact stems or additional leaves to establish opposite versus alternate attachment, rather than forcing a terminal choice.
Test the key on independently identified specimens and include clear definitions or drawings of the contrasting traits.

title: Environmental DNA with a contamination control
stem: Constructed eDNA results give barcode read counts for taxa A, B, C and D in a pond sample: 120, 30, 8 and 0. A field blank processed with it gives 0, 0, 6 and 0 reads. In this exercise a positive detection requires at least 10 sample reads and at least five times the blank count; a zero blank imposes no fold requirement. The threshold is a supplied decision rule, not a universal biological standard.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Apply the rule to identify supported detections and calculate the sample-to-blank ratio for C.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain why the data do not establish that A is four times as abundant as B in the pond.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Evaluate a claim that C and D are certainly absent.

steps.text: A and B exceed 10 reads with zero blank; C has 8 reads and 8/6 =1.33 times its blank.
A and B meet the rule; C and D do not.
Different species can release different quantities of DNA per organism.
DNA persistence, transport and sampling position affect the amount recovered.
Barcode amplification and detection efficiency can differ, so 120/30 is a read-count ratio rather than a validated organism-abundance ratio.
C is not a supported positive under the rule and has a contamination warning, but this is not proof of absence.
D could be present below detection or missed through spatial or temporal sampling.
Use independent sites/times, extraction controls and validated barcode references to improve detection confidence; stronger thresholds trade sensitivity against false positives.

title: A transferred gene is not a mating test
stem: In a constructed bacterial comparison, many core genes group lineages P and Q most closely, with R more distant. A resistance gene instead groups P with R. A separate supplied experiment shows that P can acquire this gene from R without sexual reproduction. All three lineages divide asexually. The schematic depicts gene transfer rather than a whole-organism family tree.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Explain the most direct interpretation of the discordant resistance-gene relationship.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain two difficulties in applying the biological species concept to these bacteria.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Suggest an evidence-based classification strategy and evaluate its limits.

steps.text: Horizontal transfer from R to P can make their resistance genes similar despite a different core-gene history.
A single transferred gene therefore need not represent the overall evolutionary relationship among the bacterial lineages.
The usual criterion of interbreeding and fertile offspring cannot be applied in the same way to organisms reproducing asexually.
Genes can cross lineage boundaries by horizontal transfer without sexual reproduction or formation of a hybrid organism.
A shared resistance trait can therefore occur in otherwise distinct bacterial lineages and cannot alone establish one species.
Compare many core sequences, genome-wide similarity and stable ecological or phenotypic traits rather than only the resistance gene.
Sample multiple individuals per lineage to separate within-lineage diversity from between-lineage differences.
Any operational boundary must be stated and justified; a single universal mating test or gene-similarity threshold is not demonstrated here.

title: An unresolved node is not a sequence of ancestors
stem: The constructed rooted cladogram places A outside a clade containing B, C and D. The B, C, D node is a polytomy: the available data do not resolve their branching order. Branch lengths have no time meaning. All four terminal labels represent living species.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Identify the smallest represented clade containing B and D and explain whether B is more closely related to C than to D.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Evaluate the statements “A is the ancestor of B” and “C is older than D because its branch is longer”.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Explain what additional evidence could resolve the polytomy and how it should be reported.

steps.text: The smallest represented clade containing B and D also contains C, together with their common ancestor.
The unresolved node does not establish B–C as a closer pair than B–D; all three relationships remain unresolved at that node.
A is a terminal living species, not the internal hypothetical common ancestor of B.
A and B share an earlier ancestor represented by an internal node/root.
Branch lengths were not defined as time, so graphical length cannot establish age or divergence time.
Compare informative sequences from multiple independent loci in B, C, D with an appropriate outgroup.
Assess whether a particular branching order has stronger support and examine conflicting loci or inadequate sampling.
If evidence remains insufficient, retain the polytomy rather than presenting one arbitrary binary resolution as established.

title: Parsimony with a conflicting character
stem: Three binary characters are supplied for four invented taxa. Characters 1 and 2 each have states A 0, B 0, C 1, D 1; character 3 has A 0, B 1, C 0, D 1. Treat characters as independent, equally weighted and unordered. Candidate unrooted splits are AB|CD, AC|BD and AD|BC. A compatible 2–2 pattern requires one change on its matching split and two changes on either alternative; this rule is supplied.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Calculate the total minimum changes for each candidate split and select the most parsimonious.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain why character 3 is not simply ignored and what its disagreement shows.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Evaluate whether the smallest score proves the selected evolutionary history.

steps.text: Apply one change for a matching character and two for a conflicting 2–2 character.
AB|CD requires 1 +1 +2 =4 changes; AC|BD requires 2 +2 +1 =5.
AD|BC requires 2 +2 +2 =6; AB|CD is most parsimonious under the supplied assumptions.
All three independently specified characters contribute equally to the total score.
Character 3 favours AC|BD, so the dataset contains conflicting phylogenetic signal that can be explained by repeated change, reversal or another source of disagreement.
Parsimony selects the history with fewest changes under a model; actual evolution can include extra changes or convergence.
If characters 1 and 2 were not independent, counting both at equal weight could overstate support for AB|CD.
Additional independent molecular evidence and alternative models can test whether the inferred grouping is robust.

title: Two lineages contribute to a molecular clock
stem: Constructed aligned sequences from species P and Q differ at 24 of 1000 sites. Assume differences accumulate independently at an equal rate in both lineages, with no repeated substitutions. The supplied rate is 2.0 differences per 1000 sites per million years per lineage. A plausible rate range is 1.5–2.5 under the same model. A fossil independently establishes their split occurred at least 4 million years ago.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Estimate the divergence time using the central rate and explain the factor of two.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Calculate the divergence-time range from the supplied rate bounds and compare it with the fossil minimum.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Evaluate the assumptions that limit the time estimate.

steps.text: Pairwise differences accumulate on two descendant branches, so 24 =2 ×2.0 ×t.
The estimate is 6.0 million years; using 24/2.0 would wrongly count only one accumulating lineage.
Use the fastest rate for the youngest time and slowest for the oldest: 24/(2 ×2.5) and 24/(2 ×1.5).
The range is 4.8–8.0 million years, compatible with a split at least 4 million years ago.
Rates can vary among lineages with generation time, selection and other biological factors.
Repeated substitutions can conceal earlier changes, so observed differences need not equal the total changes.
The 1000-site sample and fossil interpretation introduce additional uncertainty; the rate bounds are model inputs, not a demonstrated confidence interval.
A fossil minimum constrains the split but does not specify its exact age or calibrate every gene equally.

title: A familiar flower can mislead classification
stem: Traditional classification placed invented plants P, Q and R in family F because all have a tubular flower; S has an open flower. A constructed well-supported molecular cladogram is ((P, Q),(R, S)). Assume the root ancestor had an open flower. The diagram indicates only tip states; internal flower states have not been directly observed.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Explain why grouping P, Q and R but excluding S fails to form a clade on the supplied tree.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Give two possible evolutionary accounts of the flower pattern and explain why flower similarity alone is insufficient.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Propose a classification consistent with the molecular tree and evaluate the evidence needed before changing names.

steps.text: The most recent common ancestor of P, Q and R also has S among its descendants.
Excluding S therefore omits a descendant of that ancestor; the traditional group is not a complete clade.
Tubular flowers could have evolved separately in the P–Q lineage and in R, representing convergence.

Alternatively, from the supplied open-flowered root, tubular flowers could arise in the P–Q lineage and separately in the R–S ancestor, followed by a loss in S; this account requires three changes rather than two.
The same tip pattern can result from different histories, so a shared flower form need not uniquely establish recent ancestry.
Recognize a P–Q clade and an R–S clade, or include all four within one more inclusive clade; another complete-clade grouping is acceptable.
Confirm the inferred relationships using multiple independent sequences and appropriate taxon sampling.
Assess whether apparent molecular support is robust; a single potentially misleading locus would not justify treating reclassification as certain.

title: rRNA evidence above the kingdom level
stem: Constructed rRNA alignments compare bacteria B, archaea A and eukaryotes E. Pairwise differences per 200 sites are B–A 60, B–E 64 and A–E 28. The supplied rooted tree groups A and E after B branches off. The sequences were chosen as homologous regions, and positions with uncertain alignment were excluded. The tree is a simplified comparison, not a statement about every gene’s history.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Calculate the percentage sequence differences and identify the closest pair for this region.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain how such evidence supports distinguishing three domains rather than putting all non-nucleated organisms into one undifferentiated group.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Evaluate whether the difference counts establish exact divergence dates or equal evolutionary ranks.

steps.text: Divide each difference count by 200 and multiply by 100.
B–A =30%, B–E =32% and A–E =14%; A–E are the closest pair in this alignment.
rRNA is homologous and can be compared across widely separated cellular groups.
Sequence differences reveal deep genetic distinctions between bacterial and archaeal lineages despite shared absence of a nucleus.
A three-domain classification recognizes Bacteria, Archaea and Eukarya; a superficial structural similarity alone can conceal evolutionary differences.
Dates require calibrated rates and assumptions about change; counts alone do not supply a clock.
Taxonomic ranks are human classification categories and need not represent equal amounts of divergence.
Additional genes and taxa should test the simplified relationship, since gene transfer and sampling can alter individual gene trees.

title: The same bones, a different kind of wing
stem: The constructed schematic compares a mammal forelimb, a bird forelimb and an insect wing. In the mammal and bird, a single proximal bone leads to two bones and then digits, although proportions differ. The insect wing is an outgrowth without that internal bone pattern. Flight function is shared by the bird and insect; the mammal shown uses its forelimb for walking.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Explain which comparison supports homology and why function alone does not define it.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain in what sense the bird and insect wings are analogous, and state a qualification needed when describing the bird limb.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Evaluate the claim that the most similar overall outline must indicate the closest relationship.

steps.text: The mammal and bird forelimbs share a corresponding underlying bone arrangement inherited from a common ancestor.
Their different current functions do not remove that structural and ancestral correspondence.
Homology is based on common evolutionary origin, rather than requiring identical use or identical proportions.
Both wings serve flight, but the wing structures evolved from different ancestral structures, making flight wings analogous in this comparison.
The bird’s forelimb skeleton is still homologous with other tetrapod forelimbs; analogy for flight does not erase homology at another structural level.
Similar environments or functions can select similar forms independently, producing convergent evolution.
Compare internal anatomy, development and independent DNA/protein sequences rather than outline alone.
The diagram supports a structural comparison but does not itself quantify divergence time or determine every relationship.

title: A heritable response to selective breeding
stem: Constructed seed-mass data compare a wild population and a line selected for large seeds over six generations. Parents grown in a rich environment have mean seed masses wild 12 mg and selected 20 mg. Offspring of both are then grown in the same low-nutrient common garden: wild offspring 10 mg and selected offspring 16 mg. A separate unselected control line remains near the wild mean. No claim about a particular real crop is intended.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Calculate the percentage advantage of the selected line over the wild population in the common garden and compare the absolute differences between environments.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain how the evidence is consistent with evolution through selective breeding rather than only acquired change in individual plants.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Evaluate whether the common-garden result identifies the responsible genes or excludes every non-genetic explanation.

steps.text: Common-garden advantage =(16 −10)/10 ×100.
The advantage is 60%; absolute differences are 8 mg in the rich environment and 6 mg in the common garden.
Breeding individuals with larger seeds changes which heritable variants contribute to subsequent generations.
A difference persists in offspring grown under the same environment, supporting a heritable component rather than only the parental nutrient treatment.
The population changes over generations; an individual growing larger solely because it receives more nutrients is not itself population evolution.
The result does not identify specific DNA changes or distinguish all genetic contributions.
Maternal provisioning or other inherited environmental effects could persist into one offspring generation.
Replicate selection lines, random allocation and further common-garden generations would strengthen the heritable-selection interpretation.

title: Isolation without a geographical barrier
stem: Two constructed insect populations live in the same meadow. P adults are active mainly in spring and Q mainly in autumn. When adult emergence is synchronized experimentally, within-population courtship succeeds in 90 of 100 trials and between-population courtship in 20 of 100. The resulting interpopulation offspring, when produced, are fertile. Natural overlap in adult activity is only 5 days per year.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Calculate the reduction in successful courtship between populations relative to the within-population value.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Identify two prezygotic barriers and explain why fertile hybrids do not remove their possible effect.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Discuss whether these results establish completed sympatric speciation.

steps.text: Successful courtship is reduced by 77.8%; the raw difference is 70 successes per 100 trials.
Different adult activity seasons can create temporal isolation before mating occurs.
Lower courtship success after synchronization indicates a possible behavioural barrier.
Fertility of hybrids concerns a later stage; populations can exchange few genes because mating is restricted even if rare hybrids are fertile.
The same location is consistent with a sympatric setting, but does not prove that divergence began without past geographic isolation.
Some successful courtship and fertile hybrids indicate possible gene flow; the degree of natural reproductive isolation remains to be measured.
Measure natural mating and genetic exchange over time, controlling laboratory conditions, rather than applying an arbitrary courtship threshold for species status.

title: Resource use during adaptive radiation
stem: A constructed island lineage gives rise to three closely related bird species after colonization. Resource-use curves show species A using mainly small seeds, B medium seeds and C large seeds. Supplied historical evidence indicates that these resources were initially underused by other birds. The curves summarize diets and are not measurements of abundance or reproductive success.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Use the curves to compare the highest-use seed sizes and identify an area of diet overlap.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain how the pattern is consistent with adaptive radiation rather than three unrelated colonizations.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Evaluate what is still needed to infer that resource competition caused speciation.

steps.text: A peaks near 2 mm, B near 5 mm and C near 8 mm in the constructed data.
For example A and B overlap around 3–4 mm; use of neighbouring seed sizes is not completely exclusive.
The supplied common-lineage evidence identifies descent from one colonizing lineage.
Different heritable adaptations to available resources can be favoured in descendant populations.
Divergence into different ecological roles can reduce competition and allow multiple related species to coexist.
Present diet separation alone does not establish the historical cause or timing of reproductive isolation.
Genetic relationships, reproductive-isolation evidence and historical or experimental evidence about resource-dependent fitness would strengthen the explanation.
Curve overlap does not quantify competition without information about resource availability and demand; vacant niches are opportunities, not purposeful targets sought by evolution.

title: Chromosome doubling after plant hybridization
stem: In a constructed Persicaria model, parent P has 2n =18 and parent Q has 2n =24. Each forms balanced haploid gametes. Their hybrid receives one gamete from each parent. The parental chromosome sets are sufficiently different that most chromosomes lack pairing partners in the undoubled hybrid. A chromosome-doubling event produces two copies of each original hybrid chromosome. Assume no chromosome loss.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Calculate the chromosome counts in the parental gametes, the first hybrid and the doubled hybrid.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain why doubling can restore fertility without making the hybrid identical to either parent.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Predict the balanced gamete count of the doubled hybrid and discuss how a new lineage could become reproductively isolated.

steps.text: P gametes have 9 chromosomes and Q gametes 12; add one of each.
The initial hybrid has 21 chromosomes and the doubled hybrid 42.
In the undoubled hybrid many chromosomes lack homologous partners for regular meiosis.
Doubling supplies a partner for each chromosome, permitting more regular pairing and balanced gamete formation.
The doubled plant retains chromosome sets derived from both parents, so it is a new combination rather than simply P or Q.
A balanced gamete from the 42-chromosome doubled hybrid contains 21 chromosomes.
Crosses with P or Q would combine 21 with 9 or 12, producing 30- or 33-chromosome offspring whose pairing may be disrupted.

Reduced fertility of such crosses can limit gene flow, while fertile doubled individuals may reproduce among themselves or by suitable self-fertilization; chromosome-number difference is not an absolute guarantee of sterility in every case.

title: More citizen records, fewer sightings per hour
stem: Constructed citizen-science records for an invented wetland bird total 80, 120, 150 and 180 in years 1–4. Observer effort rises from 200 to 400, 750 and 1200 hours. parts.label: b

Train observers, validate identifications and use repeated surveys to quantify consistency and distinguish repeated observations where possible.

title: A seed bank cannot replace a habitat
stem: In a constructed programme for an endangered plant, equal samples of 200 seeds from each of ten maternal families are stored. After five years, germination is 60% for families 1–8 and 10% for families 9–10. A restored reserve supports pollinators and natural recruitment but remains vulnerable to fire. The plotted quantities are expected germinating seeds per family, not directly measured future adults.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Calculate the expected total germinating seeds and the contribution of families 9–10 as a percentage of that total.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain why a large stored total can still be a weak safeguard for genetic diversity.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Propose complementary in situ and ex situ actions and evaluate their limitations.

steps.text: Eight families contribute 8 ×200 ×0.60 =960 seeds; two contribute 2 ×200 ×0.10 =40.
The expected total is 1000; families 9–10 contribute 4.0%.
Unequal survival or germination can make some families poorly represented despite equal initial sampling.
The same number of seeds need not contain equal numbers of distinct genetic variants.
Losing rare family representation could remove variation that may matter for future adaptation or recovery.
Maintain and restore habitat, pollinators and recruitment in situ, with fire management or multiple protected sites.
Refresh or duplicate seed collections across families and storage locations, testing viability and avoiding overcollection from the wild.
Ex situ storage reduces some immediate risks but does not preserve all ecological interactions; habitat protection alone remains vulnerable to local catastrophe.

title: Forest loss and an incomplete causal story
stem: A constructed regional example is inspired by threats to Southeast Asian mixed dipterocarp forest, but the numbers do not describe a real surveyed region. Forest area in years 0, 5 and 10 is 1000, 760 and 500 km²; plantation area is 100, 300 and 520 km². A bird restricted mainly to intact forest has standardized encounter rates 24, 18 and 9 per 100 survey-hours. Roads, hunting and pesticide use also increase during the decade. Exact values are supplied so comparisons need not depend on reading the sketch.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Calculate percentage forest loss over the decade and percentage decline in bird encounter rate.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain two mechanisms by which human activities could reduce biodiversity in this setting.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Evaluate the inference that plantation expansion alone caused the entire bird decline, and propose a useful conservation response.

steps.text: Forest loss =(1000 −500)/1000 ×100; bird-rate decline =(24 −9)/24 ×100.
Forest area falls 50%; bird encounter rate falls 62.5%.
Conversion of forest to plantations removes or fragments habitat and can reduce resources for forest-dependent species.
Hunting can directly remove organisms and reduce viable breeding populations; pollution/pesticides can harm non-target organisms or food resources.
Roads may facilitate access or isolate habitat patches, connecting economic activity with further exploitation and fragmentation.
The trends are associated, but hunting, roads, pesticides or detection changes are alternative or interacting explanations.
Repeated standardized surveys across regions with differing land-use histories and measured pressures would better test mechanisms; encounter rate is not automatically absolute population size.
Protect and reconnect intact forest while addressing hunting and pollution; combine habitat conservation with targeted species measures rather than assuming one action resolves every threat.
